metadata.title: Quantitative Labeling of Sodium, Potassium, and Phosphorus for Human Over-the-Counter and Prescription Drug Products

candidates.statement: The drug labeling should state the total amount of the constituent, regardless of whether the 88 constituent is present as part of an active or inactive ingredient. The amount of sodium, 89 potassium, or phosphorus in a drug product should be determined from the drug product’s 90 formulation information. For example, if a drug product contains both naproxen sodium and 91 trisodium citrate, the total amount of sodium in the drug product from both compounds should be 92 stated. The amount of sodium present in 1 gram (g) of trisodium citrate, for instance, is 267 mg 93 as determined stoichiometrically according to its molecular formula (Na3C6H5O7). Similarly, 1 g 94 of anhydrous dibasic calcium phosphate (CaHPO4) contains 228 mg of phosphorus. 95

candidates.statement: For consistency across products and for simplicity and ease of determination, FDA recommends 115 that manufacturers provide quantitative information on a per dosage unit basis. The dosage unit 116 should be consistent with the primary expression of potency strength on the container label. For 117 oral solids, the amount per tablet, capsule, etc., should be used regardless of how many 118 tablets/capsules a patient might take at one time or per day as stated in the labeling. For oral 119 liquids (or products reconstituted to make an oral liquid), if the strength is expressed as the 120 amount of drug/mL or amount of drug/5 mL, for the purposes of reporting sodium, potassium, or 121 phosphorus, the dosage unit will be 1 mL or 5 mL, respectively. 122
candidates.context: C. Clarifying Quantities Per Dosage Unit 113 For injectable dosage forms, the dosage unit will be 1 mL, unless the net quantity in the 124 container is less than 1 mL, in which case the dosage unit will be the net quantity in the 125 container. 126

candidates.statement: FDA regulations currently require labeling of certain OTC drugs to include quantitative 155 information for sodium (21 CFR 201.64) and potassium (21 CFR 201.72). Specifically, the 156 regulations state that the labeling of OTC drug products intended for oral ingestion must contain 157 the sodium content per dosage unit (e.g., per tablet, per 5 mL), if the sodium content of a single 158 maximum recommended dose of the product (which may be one or more dosage units) is 5 mg 159 or more. The same standard applies for potassium. This information is captured under the Other 160 information heading of the Drug Facts labeling. 7
candidates.context: FDA’s labeling recommendation in this guidance for phosphorus in OTC drug products aligns 163 with the existing regulations for sodium and potassium in OTC drug products intended for oral 164 ingestion. 8 For orally ingested OTC drugs, FDA recommends (1) including the amount of 165 phosphorus in the Drug Facts labeling under the heading Other information and (2) labeling the 166 phosphorus content per dosage unit (e.g., per tablet) if the phosphorus content of a single 167 maximum recommended dose of the product (which may be one or more dosage units) is 5 mg 168 or more. See Appendix B for examples regarding this section. 169

candidates.statement: When quantitative information on sodium, potassium, and phosphorus content is included in 173 prescription drug labeling, it should be presented per dosage unit in the DESCRIPTION section 174 of labeling, following the list of inactive ingredients. See Appendix A for examples regarding 175 this section. 176
candidates.context: 2. Prescription Drug Products 171 We note that for some biological products, such as cellular therapy products, quantification may 178 be difficult. In such cases, we recommend that manufacturers considering including information 179 about these substances discuss with the appropriate FDA review division how to quantify these 180 substances. 181

candidates.statement: Generally, drug product labeling for a drug approved under an abbreviated new drug application 186 (ANDA) is required to be the same as the labeling for the RLD, with certain permissible labeling 187 differences because the ANDA and the RLD are produced or distributed by different 188 manufacturers. Permissible differences include, for example, differences in labeling made to 189 comply with current FDA labeling guidelines or other guidance (see section 505(j)(2)(A)(v) of 190 the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 355)) and 21 CFR 191 314.94(a)(8)(iv)). 192
candidates.context: F. Considerations for Generic Drugs Approved Under Section 505(j) of the 183 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 184 An ANDA or a supplement to an ANDA that proposes to include quantitative information in its 194 proposed labeling for sodium, potassium, and/or phosphorus, as recommended in this guidance, 195 or proposes to omit such quantitative information, even if the inclusion or omission of such 196 information differs from how such information is reflected in the labeling for the RLD, may be 197 acceptable, provided the requirements for approval are met. 198

candidates.statement: An applicant submitting a new drug application (NDA), an ANDA, or a biologics license 210 application (BLA) that elects to include quantitative information on sodium, potassium, or 211 phosphorus in product labeling must ensure that the labeling statement is accurate and is 212 supported by information related to the drug product’s ingredients. 9 Support for the quantitative 213 information regarding the amounts of constituents of ingredients that are described in labeling 214 should be submitted in the chemistry, manufacturing, and controls section of the application, 215 under the heading DESCRIPTION AND COMPOSITION OF THE DRUG PRODUCT. 216 Manufacturers with pending applications may add this information when they propose changes 217 to their draft labeling during the application review process. 218
